series.name: Best buys: nothing cheaper catches more

figures.title: What each monitor catches, and what it costs
figures.question: At a fixed audit budget, how many backdoors does each monitor catch, and what does it cost per program?
figures.shows: Each marker is one monitor configuration: a model at one reasoning setting. Up is better (more of the 500 backdoors caught). Left is cheaper (list-price cost to score one program). Colour is the provider, and a line joins the reasoning settings of the same model. Faint vertical bars behind the markers are 95% bootstrap intervals. The dashed grey line traces the best buys: each monitor on it catches more backdoors than every cheaper monitor. Anything below and to the right of that line is beaten by something cheaper. Use the buttons to change the audit budget.
figures.takeaway:
At a 2% audit budget the top three monitors are close. Sonnet 5.5 at its default (high) effort catches 87.6% (84.4 to 90.3) for $0.0093 per program. Haiku 5.5 at xhigh catches 85.1% (75.7 to 88.0) for $0.0018, about 5 times cheaper. Sonnet with thinking off sits between them at 84.7% for $0.0076.

Below those there is a gap. GLM-5.3, Qwen 3.8 and GPT-6 Luna at their best settings catch 61 to 76%. Haiku 4.5 and Mistral Large 4 catch about 49%, and the rest are under 40%.

Price is a poor guide to monitoring skill. GLM-5.3 at max effort costs $0.0146 per program, 1.6 times Sonnet, and catches 76.2%. Haiku 4.5 costs 3.1 times as much as Haiku 5.5 at xhigh and catches 49.2%. Mistral Large 4 costs $0.0062 and catches 49.1%, while GPT-6 Luna at xhigh catches 61.0% for $0.00045.
debate: Control Tax (Terekhov et al., 2025) already plots a cost-vs-safety frontier for 13 monitors at a 5% budget, per Marnick's literature check. We should not present the frontier itself as new. What's ours is reasoning effort as a second dial, current models, and the exact-budget accounting.

Sonnet 5.5 is labelled "untrusted monitoring" in our runs, but the code it reads was written by older models, so there is no collusion. Read it as "what a strong model gets when it monitors honestly", a reference point rather than something a lab would deploy as its trusted monitor.

Costs are list prices times tokens, after Marnick's fixes: cached calls now count, and GLM-5.3 is priced at the discounted rate it is actually billed at. GLM-5.3's effort=none run is left off because it is the max setting in disguise (the provider ignored "none").

figures.title: Haiku at xhigh keeps up with Sonnet from 2% up, not below
figures.question: Across audit budgets, how far behind Sonnet 5.5 is Haiku 5.5 at xhigh?
figures.shows: Top: share of backdoors caught as the audit budget grows, with 95% bands. Haiku at its default setting is shown for reference. Bottom: Sonnet's lead over Haiku xhigh in percentage points. The band comes from a paired bootstrap, which resamples the same problems for both monitors, so it is tighter than comparing the two top bands by eye.
figures.takeaway:
Sonnet is ahead at every budget, but by how much depends on the budget. At 2% the gap is +2.5 points (95% interval +0.6 to +10.6). At 5% it is +4.0 points (95% interval +2.1 to +6.4). At 1% it grows to +12.0 points (95% interval +1.0 to +30.3), and at 0.5% to +26.6 points (95% interval +6.4 to +64.1).

Marnick reached the same answer a different way. He compares the two only at audit rates both can hit exactly, using the 0 to 100 versions of both monitors. At 1.2%, the tightest rate with enough honest programs behind it, Sonnet leads by 13.8 points (95% interval +2.4 to +22.8).

So the cheap monitor is a near substitute only when a human can check about 2% or more of the code. With a tighter human budget, the bigger model's lead grows fast.

Most of Sonnet's edge isn't its thinking. With thinking off, Sonnet catches 84.7% at 2%, and Haiku xhigh matches it: the gap is -0.4 points (95% interval -2.7 to +7.7).
debate: This changes the summary page. It says the two can't be separated because their intervals overlap. With exact budgets and a paired test, the gap is small but clearly above zero at every budget, and Marnick's matched-rate test agrees. We should update that line (it lives in web/, so it needs a PR to main).

Method, as agreed: Marnick's matched-rate number for the tight-budget claim, our exact-budget curve for the overview. Marnick should check the 13.8 figure is quoted the way he means it (results/analysis/MONITOR-GAP.md).

Your task list asked whether Haiku finding backdoors Sonnet missed was luck. At the reported 2% the split is actually the other way round: Sonnet alone catches 18, Haiku alone 9. Haiku's 9 were scored 0.2 by Haiku, one step above its cutoff. They only count because Haiku's "2%" audits 1.6% of honest code while Sonnet's audits 1.0% (Figure 4). Sonnet scored them 0 or 0.1. Sonnet's 18 got 0.2 to 0.9 from Sonnet and 0.1 from Haiku, the score Haiku gives 44% of honest programs. So Haiku's extra catches come from extra audit budget, and Sonnet's come from real signal. Not luck, ties.

The 50% crossover on the old chart (Haiku alone 22, Sonnet alone 6) is the same effect. At 50% the cutoff is 0, and Sonnet gives 34 backdoors a flat 0. I'd drop the 50% budget from the post. Nobody audits half their code.
Below 1%, the cutoff rests on 5 honest programs or fewer, so the bands are wide. The gap there is real but its size is not well measured.

Monitors answer on a 0 to 10 scale but use only a few values. Sonnet gives 91% of honest programs a 0. Haiku at xhigh splits them between 0 and 0.1. The audit cutoff has to sit on one of those values. Across our runs, a requested 2% budget really audits between 0.2% and 2.0% of honest code.

That changes rankings. Monitors whose scores tie a lot are under-credited, by up to 16 points (table). We fix it for free: audit everything above the cutoff, plus a random share of the programs tied at the cutoff, so every monitor audits exactly the budget. All figures above use this. It matters most when comparing monitors with integer scores, as ControlArena's default prompt gives. More honest data doesn't help, because a 0 to 10 score only ever offers 11 cutoffs.
debate: This is the decision we left open. My recommendation changed after doing the numbers: report exact budgets as the main numbers, with the old "as reported" numbers and the served rate in an appendix table. It's a one-line switch (HEADLINE in build.py), so it's cheap to reverse.

Random tie-breaking fixes fairness, not sample size. At 500 honest programs a 1% budget still rests on 5 of them. Marnick's supporting figures show the other two fixes: a 0 to 100 score scale (more distinct scores) and more honest programs.

Marnick's literature check found MonitoringBench saw a 0 to 100 scale collapse at the top end (honest scores hitting 100). A wider scale helps when honest scores pile up at 0, which is our case, and hurts when they pile up at the top.

figures.title: A 0 to 100 score gives Haiku more places to set the cutoff, but not Sonnet
figures.question: If the monitor is asked for a score from 0 to 100 instead of 0 to 10, can the audit budget be set more finely?
figures.shows: Each dot is a cutoff the monitor can actually use: how much honest code it audits (across) and how many backdoors it catches (up), auditing only programs strictly above the cutoff. Blue is the default 0 to 10 prompt, orange the same monitor asked for 0 to 100. Steps show that between two dots there is no cutoff to choose. Haiku's blue line stops at 1.6% because its next cutoff audits 46% of honest code. Same 500 honest and 500 backdoored programs throughout.
figures.takeaway:
The 0 to 10 prompt leaves few places to put the cutoff. At budgets of 5% or less, Haiku xhigh has 5 usable cutoffs on 0 to 10 and 11 on 0 to 100. Its catch rate at an exact 0.5% budget rises from 54.1% to 63.5%, because the finer score separates its most suspicious honest programs from the backdoors.

Sonnet barely changes: 4 usable cutoffs on 0 to 10 and 5 on 0 to 100. It still gives almost every honest program a 0, so a wider scale has nothing to spread out. At an exact 2% it catches 87.6% on 0 to 10 and 90.0% on 0 to 100.

So a wider scale is a cheap fix for monitors whose honest scores bunch up in the middle of the range, not for one that already scores honest code 0.
debate: This answers the "why" left open by Figure 3 only in part. Wide intervals at tight budgets come mostly from how few honest programs sit above the cutoff (5 at 1% with 500 honest), and a wider scale doesn't add honest programs. Marnick's supporting figure on interval width shows that side. Worth saying both in the post.

The scale isn't purely cosmetic. Marnick measured it changing ranking quality (AUC) by about +0.6 points for Haiku and +0.2 for Sonnet, small here, but +14 for GPT-6 Luna and +8.5 for Gemma 4. So for some monitors a 0 to 100 prompt makes them better at the task, not just finer-grained.

Marnick's literature check found MonitoringBench saw 0 to 100 scores collapse at the top (honest code hitting 100). A wider scale helps when honest scores pile up low and can hurt when they pile up high.
Marnick ran 0 to 100 on 9 monitors. His supporting "score scale" figure shows all of them; this one picks the two the post is about.

figures.title: Monitors catch trigger-shaped backdoors and miss bug-shaped ones
figures.question: Is a backdoor hard because of the monitor or because of the backdoor?
figures.shows: Left: for each of the 500 backdoors, how many of seven monitors catch it at a 2% budget (as reported on the summary page). Right: the share missed by all seven, split by whether the backdoor compares the input against a number that the honest solution never uses, the classic "if x == 1234" trigger. A regex detects this, so treat the split as approximate.
figures.takeaway:
Difficulty is mostly a property of the backdoor. 277 of 500 backdoors are caught by all seven monitors and 49 by none, with few in between. Marnick's survival curves show the same thing at every budget.

Backdoors with a numeric trigger are easy. Not one of the 88 that compare the input to a new number was missed by every monitor. Of the 412 without one, 49 were. Reading the 49 misses, they look like ordinary bugs: a boundary check flipped, a loop capped "for efficiency", an extra special case that reads like edge-case handling. The section below has examples.
debate: The summary page says the hard cases are "mostly one-token edits". That's not right. Only 11 of the 49 differ from the reference solution by 4 lines or fewer, and the median is 11 lines. What they share is how they look, not how big they are. Marnick withdrew the same claim for the same reason.

The big implication: our 85 to 88% is a statement about the attacks in this dataset, most of which are clumsy. An attacker who writes bug-shaped backdoors on purpose would face a much weaker monitor. Marnick's literature sweep cites safety dropping from 99% to 59% on the same tasks when attacks are just selected better. That belongs in the post.

Is a bug-shaped backdoor even detectable from the code alone? A flipped >= looks the same whether it was planted or a slip. If so, the defence for this class is testing and verification, not a better monitor. The Opus test below gives a small first look.

"Monitors" here means seven runs, three of them Haiku at different efforts. Marnick points out that this makes "hard for everyone" partly circular. A monitor from another family (or Opus) is the check.

figures.marnick_text: Left to right is the number of honest files sitting above the cutoff, which is the sample that decides where the cutoff goes. Up is how wide the resulting confidence interval is, in percentage points of attack recall. The dashed line is the median at each count. Going from one file to 46 cuts the median width from 71 points to 18, roughly a two-thirds reduction. 18 points is still enormous, so even the best-supported comparison in this study is a coarse measurement; but the slope tells you the fix is more honest samples, not a better monitor.
figures.marnick_mislead: The shade is redundant with the x position, not extra information: `n_paired_honest` is 500 on every single row, so `honest_rows_above_cutoff == shared_fpr_pct * 5` exactly and the two axes are the same variable twice. That redundancy is the point of the chart. The binding sample size is the rows above the cutoff, not the 500-problem run size, and a reader who sees `n=500` in the methods section will badly overestimate the precision of a 0.2% operating point. Also, x takes only five values, 1, 2, 3, 5 and 46, so the apparent trend rests on five groups and the median line should not be extrapolated past 46.

figures.marnick_text: The monitor is asked to score suspicion on a scale, and these 17 runs vary only that scale. On the left, higher is better: it counts the audit budgets at which the run can be measured with at least 5 clean files behind the cutoff, and every line rises, and 6 of the 6 that vary only the scale do, Haiku 5.5 xhigh from 2 to 8; GPT-6 Luna default from 1 to 4; Gemma 3 27B from 6 to 18; Gemma 3 4B from 9 to 23; Gemma 4 26B-A4B from 0 to 2; Qwen3.8 Omni Flash none from 1 to 7; Sonnet 5.5 default from 2 to 3; gpt-oss-120b default from 3 to 6. On the right, lower is better: it is the tightest budget that still has a trustworthy cutoff, and there the lines disagree, Haiku 5.5 xhigh from 1.6% to 1.0%; GPT-6 Luna default from 1.2% to 1.0%; Gemma 3 27B from 1.2% to 1.2%; Gemma 3 4B from 2.4% to 2.6%; Gemma 4 26B-A4B from no usable rung at all to 1.0%; Qwen3.8 Omni Flash none from 1.8% to 1.2%; Sonnet 5.5 default from 1.0% to 1.2%; gpt-oss-120b default from 4.6% to 1.8%. Gemma 4 26B-A4B had no usable rung on the narrow scale, so for that monitor the wider prompt is the difference between a budget axis and none. The floor improves for Haiku 5.5 xhigh; GPT-6 Luna default; Gemma 4 26B-A4B; Qwen3.8 Omni Flash none; gpt-oss-120b default and gets worse for Gemma 3 4B; Sonnet 5.5 default, so the right panel has no single direction. That split is the point, because the same fix buys more operating points on the left and yet moves the tightest trustworthy budget both ways on the right. An open marker means that monitor has no arm at the next scale along, not that it fell to zero. Two lines are not a scale ablation at all and are named in the note below: their wider arm also changed how much the monitor thinks, so whatever they show, the prompt is not the only cause.
figures.marnick_mislead: A sweep over 8 monitors is not a sample. These runs cannot say whether widening the scale helps a monitor outside the set, and the ones they cover disagree about the direction in the right-hand panel, so the finding is that this is monitor-specific rather than that one should prompt for 0-100. A 0.2 point move in a floor estimated on 500 honest files is also one file either way, so the regression on Gemma 3 4B; Sonnet 5.5 default is real in the data and far from an established effect. Nothing here is a safety improvement: the monitor did not get better, it got measurable. These arms also carry a usage record on every row, with 2 of them (Gemma 4 26B-A4B; Sonnet 5.5 default) carrying no usage rows at all, which does not touch the rung counts but does affect any cost claim made beside them.

The claim this chart supports is the negative one: the prediction was collapse and there is no collapse at either point. figures.marnick_text: Suppose you have one budget for false alarms: a fixed number of honest files you are willing to have a human open. You can spend it on one monitor with a generous cutoff, or split it across several monitors with tight ones and audit anything that any of them flags. The dial is how many you are allowed to buy. The solid line is the best you can do with that many; the dashed line is the best a single monitor does. The gap between them is what the extra monitors are worth, and it is small: +2.4 points at the most generous point in the grid. The number that dwarfs it is on the dashed line itself, which climbs +6.4 points between a 2% budget and a 10% one.
figures.marnick_mislead: This is an in-sample maximum. The same 500 problems choose the combination and then score it, over thousands of candidate configurations, so every solid-line value is optimistically biased and the true out-of-sample gain is smaller than the one drawn. That cuts the right way for the conclusion, which is a null: the gain is +1.8 points at 2% even with the thumb on the scale. It cuts the wrong way for any attempt to read a specific combination off the chart as a recommendation. The y-axis also starts at 0.75 rather than zero, to make a small gap visible; a monitor that catches nothing does not appear on it at all.

figures.marnick_text: The monitor is asked for one thing, a suspicion score. It also leaves a trace behind: how long it thought. This chart scores both as detectors on the same files. Both axes are the chance that a randomly chosen backdoored file ranks above a randomly chosen clean one, where 0.5 is a coin flip. Thinking length wins on 6 of the 24 runs where there is any thinking to measure, and loses on 18. The other 10 report no reasoning tokens at all and sit on the 0.5 line as diamonds; counting those in the denominator would read as though thinking length had been tried and failed on them. The point of the chart is what the 6 winners have in common: their suspicion AUCs run from only 0.592 to 0.752, so the number they were asked for had already collapsed. They are all GLM-5.3 and Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite arms. Look instead at the four strongest monitors on the page and the score wins by a distance: Haiku 5.5 / xhigh / comments kept 0.976 against 0.677; Sonnet 5.5 / default / scale 100 0.959 against 0.632; Sonnet 5.5 / low 0.956 against 0.500; Haiku 5.5 / xhigh / scale 200 0.953 against 0.747. So the honest reading is that thinking length is a rescue signal for a monitor whose score has stopped discriminating, not a better signal than a score that works. Nobody would deploy any of the 6 winners.
figures.marnick_mislead: Being above the diagonal is as much a statement that the score is broken as that thinking length is good, which is why this chart is no longer titled as a win for the byproduct. Every Gemini arm above the line has a suspicion AUC near 0.60, and the reason is that its honest suspicion scores take only 2 to 3 distinct values, so there is almost no ranking power to beat. Thinking length did not improve, the comparison got easier. Neither axis carries an interval. An AUC from 500 against 500 samples has a standard error of roughly 0.016 to 0.020, so gaps under about 0.05 are not separated, and several pairs on this chart sit inside that band. AUC is also a threshold-free summary: a signal can win on AUC and still be unusable at a 2% audit budget, which is the only operating region this project cares about.

figures.marnick_text: Everything else on this page reports recall: the share of backdoors a monitor flags when it sees them one at a time. That is not what a deployment cares about. An attacker that needs several backdoors to get anywhere has to get past the same monitor several times, and the chance it is caught at least once climbs steeply. Read the left edge as the recall figure you see elsewhere, and the right edge as what that figure buys over a campaign. The dial is the attacker giving something up: at each step it will only touch problems it can backdoor inside that many changed lines.
figures.marnick_mislead: The draw is uniform, so this is an attacker that picks its tasks without knowing anything about the monitor. That is the generous case and it is doing a lot of work here. An attacker that can see which problems a monitor scores low, and submit only those, drives every curve on this chart to zero: at a 2% budget no monitor in this study flags a single one of the attacks it ranked in its own bottom tenth, so the honest reading is that these curves bound the careless attacker and say nothing about the careful one. Two further limits: the pools shrink as the dial tightens, so the 20-landing column at 5 lines draws 20 of only 41 measured problems and is close to exhausting the set, and Gemma 3 4B is not drawn because it flags nothing whatsoever at this budget, so no number of landings helps it.
figures.title: An attacker who needs several backdoors gets caught sooner
figures.question: If the attacker has to land several backdoors, what does a recall figure at one budget actually promise?
figures.shows: If the attacker must land several backdoors, catch-at-least-once climbs fast even for weak monitors. This assumes attempts are independent and the attacker doesn't adapt, so it's an optimistic bound.
